title: Dreams in prison (Genesis 40)
hook: the butler and the baker; the butler forgets him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Potiphar's house: falsely accused, sent to prison, and still the LORD was with Joseph. Your line: good in the pit too.

I'll put in a word for you. I'll send your résumé along. I won't forget this. Everyone has had a friend who promised, and then, nothing. Not cruelty. They just got busy with their own good news. In Joseph's prison, two new men arrive from Pharaoh's own household: the chief butler, who pours Pharaoh's wine, and the chief baker. Both have fallen out of favor. One morning Joseph, who is looking after them, notices that they both look miserable.
screen: `I WON'T FORGET THIS.` → `THE BUTLER AND THE BAKER.` → `TWO SAD FACES IN THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Start with what Joseph does first. He notices. A prisoner himself, falsely accused, he still looks at the faces around him and asks, why do you look so sad today? We each had a dream, they say, and there's nobody to interpret it. Joseph answers: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" Tell me. The butler dreams of a vine with three branches; the grapes ripen, and he squeezes them into Pharaoh's cup. Joseph says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you your job back. Then he asks for one thing. Remember me when it goes well for you. Mention me to Pharaoh. I was stolen from my land, and here too I've done nothing to deserve this dungeon. The baker, encouraged, tells his dream: three baskets of bread on his head, and birds eating from the top one. Joseph's answer is grim: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head too, but off of you. Three days later, on Pharaoh's birthday, it all happens exactly as Joseph said. Then the chapter ends with one of the loneliest verses in the Torah: "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgot him." It says it twice, remember and forget, as if to let it sink in. Two more full years go by. A midrash reads those two years as a lesson for Joseph himself, about putting too much hope in a man. But you can read the verse the other way too: as a lesson for the butler, and for anyone who ever got out and left someone behind.
screen: `JOSEPH NOTICES TWO SAD FACES.` · `DO NOT INTERPRETATIONS BELONG TO GOD?` · `THREE DAYS: ONE RESTORED, ONE HANGED.` · `THE BUTLER FORGOT HIM.` · then, large: `REMEMBER ME.`

segments.voice: Think back to a hard stretch in your life and someone who helped you through it: a teacher, a neighbor, a friend who gave you a couch, or a reference, or just time. Picture their face, remember exactly what they did, and ask yourself whether they know it mattered.
Dreams in prison. Joseph reads the dreams of the butler and the baker, asks to be remembered, and is forgotten for two more years.
Your line: don't forget Joseph. The butler did, for two whole years. See you at Pharaoh's court tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls gratitude hakarat ha-tov, recognizing the good, and teaches that forgetting a kindness done to you is a real failing; the butler is the classic example.

original.note: Hebrew: to remember. the chapter ends with this word and its opposite, shakhach, to forget.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about reading dreams.
what it means: a story about noticing, and about remembering. Joseph notices two sad faces; the butler forgets the man who helped him.
what a scholar hears: 40:23 says it twice, did not remember and forgot. Genesis Rabbah 89 reads the two extra years as a lesson for Joseph about trusting in a man.
